newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. rejected Bonn deal with Colombia drug lords.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rejected Bonn deal with Colombia drug lords.

text.p: The German government asked the United States last July to join talks to broker a "peace deal" between the Colombian government and the country's drug kingpins, U.S. ambassador Myles Frechette said in an interview Sunday.

German spymaster Bernd Schmidbauer, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's head of intelligence services, sketched out plans for negotiations aided by shadowy private eye Werner Mauss, who was arrested as he tried to smuggle a rebel kidnap victim out of Colombia in November.

Frechette said the United States rejected the proposed deal with the heads of the mighty Cali drug cartel, said by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration to supply 80 percent of the world's cocaine.
He also denied Colombian press reports late last year that Kohl had held talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton, at Bogota's request, in a bid to defuse tense U.S.-Colombian relations.

"(Schmidbauer) sent emisaries to ask the American government if it was willing to see talks (with the heads of the Cali cartel). We replied in an official statement that we weren't," Frechette told Colombia's leading El Tiempo newspaper.

The U.S. envoy did not mention the terms of the German proposal. But Colombian press reports late last year said Colombian official negotiator Carlos Villamil Chaux had discussed with Germany the possibility of drug lords surrendering in exchange for light jail terms, guarantees against extradition and the confiscation of a small part of their illicit earnings.

The United States has consistently pressed for the extradition of Colombia's top drug lords and expressed outrage at the lightweight jail terms handed down to the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers, former heads of the Cali cartel, Friday. With reductions for entering guilty pleas and time off for good behaviour, the pair will walk free in less than five years.
News of the proposed deal with drug lords, which was scrapped after the U.S. rejection, only filtered out after Mauss was captured near Medellin in mid-November.

The Bonn government said Mauss, a private detective with close links to Germany's secret services, was on a "humanitarian mission" to free Brigitte Schoene, a German snatched from her home near Medellin by a suspected rebel commando in August.
He was also trying to set up peace talks between the government and the National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrilla force, Bonn said.
The Colombian authorities, however, say Mauss is an international member of the ELN and took a direct role in Schoene's kidnap.
"If it is true what they say Mauss was doing then this is terrible for foreigners living in Colombia," Frechette said.
